paras: The lynching of Jeff Curry was the killing of a Black man who was taken from two officers escorting him to jail in Birmingham, Alabama, and shot dead on the road in March 1888. Wire reports placed the killing on Sunday night, March 18, after a dispute with a white man named Powell led to Curry's arrest. Within a week four white men, among them Powell and men who had Curry in charge, were jailed as his murderers, and one paper called it the first time in the state that white men had been held for lynching a Black man.

The wire described Curry as a "negro" who worked in the Blue Creek mines, a few miles from Birmingham; a special dispatch to the Memphis Appeal called him a cobbler and placed the quarrel near Bessemer. In the wire version, Curry had a dispute with a miner named Powell, "no blows were exchanged," and Powell then had him arrested for carrying concealed weapons. The Appeal's correspondent wrote instead that two Powells, father and son, fell out with Curry over a job he had done, and that pistols were drawn on both sides but not fired.
A brief in the Pembina Pioneer Express at the end of the month said Curry had sworn to kill Powell, hid with a shotgun by the road, and was committed to jail for attempted murder.

According to the Appeal, Curry was taken before a magistrate, who ordered him sent to the Birmingham jail and appointed two white men to escort him. The Maysville Evening Bulletin named the officers as Dave Rainey and Sam Reddon; a later Appeal dispatch said Jim Day and Rainey had Curry in charge. In the wire account, the officers set out after dark and, at a deserted spot in the road, were attacked by a mob of unknown men who led the prisoner aside and shot him dead.

The Pioneer Express said "a dozen masked men" surrounded the constables and tied Curry to a tree before shooting him. The Evening Bulletin counted eleven bullet holes in the body; the Appeal said it was found with "a handful of buckshot in it."

An inquest before the same magistrate, the Appeal said, brought out nothing as to who did the shooting. The guards said disguised men had taken their prisoner, but the Appeal reported that one guard had been seen consulting a Powell just before setting out, and that the Powells' friends had been overheard planning to shoot Curry from behind a rock on the road. Warrants were sworn out for several men named in the neighborhood.

On March 25, Frank Powell, Jim Day, Dave Rainey and Sam Redden, all white, were brought to Birmingham from the Bessemer neighborhood and jailed as the murderers. The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian reported that a preliminary trial ended with all four committed without bail to await the grand jury. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict appears in the coverage after that hearing.

Most papers ran a single Birmingham dispatch, some via Chicago, on March 20 and 21, from Washington to San Antonio, Richmond, Indianapolis, New York and Savannah. The text barely varied, but the headlines did: the Washington Evening Star said a mob had riddled a Black man "who had committed no crime," the Savannah Morning News called it "An Inexcusable Lynching," and the San Antonio Daily Light headed it "Another Diabolical Negro Murder." Others used plainer headings such as "Killed by a Mob" and "Negro Prisoner Murdered."

A condensed telegram in Mississippi and Alabama weeklies called the killers "a mob of white men." The Appeal's own correspondent was the most skeptical of the officers, heading his report "Peculiar Justice. How a Negro Was Served by Alabama Officials." The claim that Curry had planned to kill the Powells appeared only after the arrests, in the Appeal's March 26 dispatch and the Pioneer Express.

The date varies: Sunday night in the wire and the Maysville dispatch, "yesterday morning" for the quarrel in the Appeal's March 19 dispatch, the 19th in the condensed telegram, and Monday night in the Asheville Citizen. The two Birmingham-dated dispatches, written within a day or two, both point to Sunday, March 18.

reader.title: Lynching of Jeff Curry
bases: Curry was taken from two officers escorting him to jail and shot dead by a group the papers called a mob (A1, A2, A6), and four men were later held for 'the lynching' (A23).

A prisoner under arrest on a criminal charge was seized from his escort and shot by a 'mob' described as a dozen masked or disguised men (A1, A2, A24); four white men were committed without bail for 'the lynching' (A19, A23), though the Memphis Appeal suggested a private quarrel with the Powells lay behind it (A2).

The Birmingham wire (A1), a separate Maysville dispatch (A6) and the Memphis Appeal's own correspondent (A2) independently agree that Curry was taken from two escorts and shot; they differ on the cause of the arrest and the date.

accounts.gist: After a dispute with miner Powell in which no blows were struck, Powell had Curry arrested for carrying concealed weapons; a mob of unknown men took him from two officers on the road Sunday night and shot him dead.

framing.detail: The Evening Star's headline said the mob riddled a Black man 'who had committed no crime'; the Savannah Morning News called it 'An Inexcusable Lynching'.
The Memphis Appeal's special, 'Peculiar Justice. How a Negro Was Served by Alabama Officials,' suspected the guards of complicity.
Most papers ran the wire under headings such as 'Shot by a Mob', 'Killed by a Mob' and 'Negro Prisoner Murdered'.
Later briefs repeated the claim that Curry had lain in ambush for Powell without attribution beyond 'it was said'.
